claimed.text: Moore told the MUFON symposium on 1 July 1989 that he had cooperated with Air Force counterintelligence from about 1980 and knowingly passed false information to Bennewitz; the board treats this as the clearest admission in the affair, a civilian speaking about himself, in public, never retracted.

Doty has said he was tasked with hoaxing documents and feeding false information to UFO researchers, that he was ordered to make Bennewitz believe in an alien invasion, and that he passed fabricated material on crash retrievals and a programme called Aquarius; the reported admission is paraphrased throughout and never quotes him.

Howe says Doty showed her at Kirtland in April 1983 a paper describing US recovery of craft and biological entities, which she could read but not copy; Cooper's 1989 paper records her telling him so, which corroborates the telling by 1989 and nothing about the document.
Bishop says he was told that the Air Force flew Bennewitz by helicopter to Archuleta Mesa and showed him a site dressed with props to draw his attention away from Kirtland.
Two fragments of Bennewitz's own 1981 report were read: that they tend to lie but their memory for lying is not long, and that they must be made to come down and destruct themselves.

Press reporting says Air Force personnel in classified units were briefed into a fictitious reverse-engineering programme called Yankee Blue and bound by NDAs, and that AARO uncovered the practice and a 2023 memorandum ordered it stopped; the Pentagon first denied any such memo, then reopened its search.
Doty says Jaime Shandera, the later recipient of the MJ-12 film, was a Naval Investigative Service asset shortly before it arrived; Doty is the sole source.

On the board's reading, the operation shows a counterintelligence element treating civilian observation over a nuclear storage site as a problem for deception rather than investigation, and Bennewitz's technical capability, not his beliefs, is what made him worth a multi-year effort.

contested.text: Doty has also denied the harm: asked by George Knapp, he called the story that he drove Bennewitz mad false in every aspect and said Bennewitz did it to himself. On the board's reading, a self-described disinformation officer's statements, including his denials, establish only what he said.

Bishop's book is a participant account at one remove: a writer relying on it reports that Bishop had an undisclosed friendship with Moore, so it should never be the sole source for a claim about Moore's conduct. Bishop himself limits what he knows Moore did to handing over the Aquarius document.
No copy of any document given to Bennewitz, and no copy of the Aquarius paper, has been opened; Howe's notes are the only record of its text.
The board records a date discrepancy in the complaint form itself: 9 September 1980 in one rendering and 2-9 Sept 80 in the NICAP page, with file number, agent and observers matching.

The Yankee Blue link rests on press reporting and inference: the claim that AARO acknowledged it in Volume I does not survive a full-text check, and the board's tie from Doty's method to Yankee Blue is about method, not about his involvement.

On the board's reading, the MJ-12 documents are an artefact of the same Albuquerque disinformation activity, but the link between the Aquarius paper and the MJ-12 film rests on timing and shared contacts, not a document.

lead.text: In August 1980 security police guarding the Manzano nuclear weapons storage area at Kirtland AFB reported lights and objects they could not identify, and an Air Force Office of Special Investigations file was opened. The Albuquerque physicist Paul Bennewitz, who was filming lights over the base, then became, by the later public admissions of William Moore and Richard Doty, the target of an Air Force disinformation effort; AARO's historical report does not mention it.

record.text: The AFOSI complaint form, filed by Special Agent Richard C. Doty of Det 1700 at Kirtland under District File No. 8017D93-0/29, documents sightings between 8 August and 3 September 1980; the named observers are SSgt Stephen Ferenz, ATC Martin W. Rist and AMN Anthony D. Frazier of the 1608 Security Police Squadron, at about 23:50 on 8 August.

The form records a bright light making stop-and-go manoeuvres near the Manzano test range that landed in Coyote Canyon and left vertically at high speed, and a Sandia security guard who saw a round disc-shaped object near an alarmed structure at about 00:20 on 9 August while his radio malfunctioned; further observations followed on 10 and 22 August.

An AFOSI record dated 10 November 1980 documents the security police observations over Coyote Canyon and the Manzano area and notes Bennewitz's photography and reporting; the file for 1980-1983 was released under FOIA and is archived by NICAP. AFOSI is the Air Force's felony investigative and counterintelligence agency, with units at most Air Force bases.
Doty's later New Mexico State Police personnel file, 321 pages, was released with redactions in 2021 under the state's public records act after federal channels had produced nothing.
Bennewitz's burial record shows a Second World War Coast Guard seaman, born 1927 and died 2003, buried at Santa Fe National Cemetery.

The National Archives searched NSC policy paper and minute indexes for MJ-12, Majestic, UFO, extraterrestrial biological entities and Aquarius, among other terms, and found nothing except one 1954 memorandum.

AARO's 2024 historical record report, Volume I, contains no mention of Kirtland, AFOSI, Bennewitz or Doty, and no occurrence of Yankee Blue; AFOSI told a FOIA requester it found no records tied to Yankee Blue, and the Pentagon's spokesperson said she could not confirm the memo described in the press.

summary.text: Bennewitz ran Thunder Scientific, an instrumentation firm with Air Force customers, from a property overlooking the east side of the base; he dated his own study to July 1979, contacted the base in October 1980 and briefed Kirtland officials on 10 November 1980.

On the board's reading of the admissions, AFOSI both investigated the 1980 intrusions and ran the operation against Bennewitz. Howe says Doty showed her a Project Aquarius paper at Kirtland in 1983; on the board's reading the MJ-12 film, postmarked Albuquerque twenty months later, came through the same channel.

Bennewitz's own late-1981 report, Project Beta, is the claimant's dated statement of his claim, and Norio Hayakawa's chronology makes him the origin point of the Dulce Base story; Greg Bishop's 2005 book of the same name is the principal account of the affair. Adam Gorightly's 2021 book on the disinformation of the period obtained Tal Levesque's confession that the Dulce insider was his invention.

The board places the alleged Yankee Blue practice, in which Air Force personnel were reportedly briefed into a fictitious programme, in the same lineage of manufacturing UFO belief for security purposes, while noting that no document ties it to Kirtland.
